7380:
The most precise and important meaning of "to hackle" is: to comb and separate plant fibers by pulling them through a sharp-toothed tool.

Here's the picture: Imagine you've harvested flax or hemp plants and you want to turn them into thread so you can weave linen cloth. The raw plant fibers are a messy tangle — mixed lengths, knotted, full of bits of plant waste. Before you can spin them into thread, you need to clean them up.

You do this by dragging the fibers through a tool that is also called a hackle — a flat board studded with many long, sharp metal teeth pointing upward, like a very aggressive comb. As you pull the fiber bundle through these teeth, two things happen at once: the teeth catch and hold back the short, tangled, useless bits (called tow), while the long, smooth, even fibers pass through and come out clean, straight, and ready for spinning.

That action — pulling fibers through the hackle tool — is "to hackle."

Think of it like detangling a badly knotted ball of string, where the knots and short bits get snagged and removed, and only the long, useful strands make it through. Or think of brushing impossibly matted hair until it's silky and smooth — except the "hair" is a plant fiber and the "brush" is a board of metal spikes.

Example in a sentence:
"Every morning she would hackle the flax before sitting down to spin."
A Secondary Meaning — To Cut Roughly

"Hackle" can also mean to cut or chop something in a rough, jagged, uneven way — not a clean cut, but a crude hacking motion. This meaning overlaps closely with the word "hack." If you hackle something in this sense, you are tearing into it more than slicing it.

Example in a sentence:
"He tried to hackle through the rope with a blunt knife."

This meaning is older and less common today, but you may encounter it in historical writing or literature.
A Third Meaning — Tying Fishing Flies

In the craft of making artificial fishing flies by hand, to hackle a fly means to wind special feathers — taken from the neck of a rooster or other bird, and called hackle feathers — tightly around the body of a hand-tied hook. These feathers fan out and mimic the look of an insect's legs or wings, making the fake fly convincing enough to fool a fish.

Example in a sentence:
"She hackled the fly with a single brown feather and tied it off."
A Note on "Heckle" — A Related Word Worth Knowing

You may know the word "heckle" — as in, to heckle a politician by shouting rude questions and interruptions at them from the crowd. That word comes directly from "hackle." The connection is vivid: just as a hackle picks apart raw fiber, a heckler picks apart what someone says, pulling out weak points and rough edges to embarrass them. In older texts, you may occasionally see "hackle" used with this exact same meaning of verbal harassment. Today, though, "heckle" handles that job entirely, while "hackle" stays in the world of fibers and feathers.
The Unifying Idea Behind All Three Meanings

Look at all three meanings together and you'll see one underlying thread:

  • Combing fibers → working through something with sharp, picking, separating action
  • Cutting roughly → attacking something with a crude, tearing motion
  • Tying flies → working fine material carefully with a combing, winding technique

In every case, "to hackle" involves a hands-on, working-through-something action — whether you're pulling fiber through teeth, hacking at material, or winding a feather around a hook.
How Common Is the Verb Today?

As a verb, "hackle" is not a word you'll hear in everyday conversation. It is mostly found in:

  • Historical writing about textile production and linen-making traditions
  • Books and guides about traditional fiber arts and hand-spinning
  • Fly-fishing manuals and craft guides

As a noun, "hackle" is far more visible — especially in the everyday phrase "raise someone's hackles," which means to make a person irritated or defensively angry. This comes from the literal hackle feathers on the back of a dog's or rooster's neck, which stand up stiffly when the animal feels threatened. When you see that phrase, you now know its roots go all the way back to the same word you've just learned.
7381:
Hackles are the hairs (or feathers, in birds) that run along the back of the neck — and sometimes down the spine — of certain animals. Think of a dog, a cat, a wolf, or a rooster. That strip of fur or feathers sitting on the back of their neck? That's the hackles.

The most important thing to understand about hackles is what they do: they stand up and bristle when the animal is angry, scared, or feeling threatened. You've probably seen a dog's fur spike up along its neck when it senses danger — that's the hackles rising. A rooster fluffs up the feathers around its neck when it's about to fight — same thing.

So in its most literal sense, hackles = the fur or feathers on the back of the neck/spine that rise up as a physical sign of alarm, aggression, or tension.

• Dogs and wolves: A ridge of stiff fur rises from the neck down toward the shoulders. This is often the clearest and most famous example.
  • Cats: Similar raised fur along the spine and neck — this is why an alarmed cat looks like it suddenly doubled in size.
  • Roosters and fighting birds: The long, flowing feathers around the neck flare outward dramatically. In fact, these neck feathers on a rooster are called hackles specifically, even when they're not raised. Fly fishermen actually use rooster hackle feathers to tie artificial fishing flies.
The Figurative Meaning (How It Applies to People)

This is where the word becomes truly useful in everyday English, because people use "hackles" to describe human anger and irritation too — through a handful of very common phrases.

The idea is borrowed from animals: just as a dog's hackles rise when it feels threatened or provoked, a person's metaphorical hackles rise when they feel annoyed, defensive, or angry.

"To raise someone's hackles"

This is the single most common phrase. It means to annoy, irritate, or offend someone — to provoke a defensive or angry reaction in them.

"His rude tone immediately raised her hackles."
(= His rudeness made her feel irritated and defensive.)

"That politician's speech raised hackles across the country."
(= It angered and offended many people.)

"Someone's hackles rose / are up"

This describes the state of being already annoyed or ready to react aggressively.

"His hackles rose the moment they walked into the room."
(= He immediately became tense, wary, and irritated.)

"She walked into the meeting with her hackles up."
(= She was already defensive and on edge before anything even happened.)

"With hackles raised"

Used to describe someone who is visibly agitated, defensive, or ready to argue.

"He responded to the criticism with hackles raised."
(= He replied in an angry, defensive manner.)

Whether you're talking about an animal or a person, hackles are always about threat, tension, and defensive aggression. The image is the same: something provokes a reaction, and the body (literally or figuratively) bristles in response. The raised hackles of a growling dog is the perfect physical picture of what the word always means, even when used about humans.

LiterallyThe fur/feathers on the back of an animal's neck that bristle when the animal is threatened or aggressive
FigurativelyUsed in phrases to describe human irritation, anger, or defensiveness
Key phrase"raise someone's hackles" = to irritate or offend someone
Core feelingThreat → tension → bristling defensiveness
One Sentence to Remember It Forever

Hackles are the hairs on the back of a dog's neck that stand up when it's ready to growl — and in everyday English, "raising someone's hackles" means making them feel that same bristling, defensive irritation.
7382:
Something is hackneyed when it has been used so many times that it has completely lost its freshness, power, and impact. What was once an interesting or meaningful phrase, idea, or expression has become flat, dull, and predictable — simply because too many people have repeated it too many times.

Think of it this way: the first person who said "time heals all wounds" was expressing a genuine and moving insight. But after millions of people repeated it in books, speeches, greeting cards, and conversations for decades, the phrase stopped making anyone pause and think. It just passes through the mind without leaving a mark. That is a hackneyed expression.
The most important thing to understand

Hackneyed does not mean something was always bad. It means something became bad through overuse. The idea or phrase was probably meaningful when it first appeared. The problem is that its endless repetition drained it of all its life and impact. This is what separates hackneyed from simply "wrong" or "bad."
What kinds of things can be hackneyed?

Mostly language and ideas — phrases and expressions like "think outside the box" or "at the end of the day," story plots like the reluctant hero who saves the world at the last second, metaphors like "life is a journey," or arguments and excuses that feel overly familiar because everyone reaches for them automatically.

Hackneyed is a criticism. When you call something hackneyed, you are saying: "This lacks originality. The person who used this phrase or idea didn't think freshly — they just grabbed the nearest ready-made expression." It suggests laziness of thought or language. It's not a savage insult, but in the world of writing, speaking, and ideas, it's a meaningful one.

"The film's plot was completely hackneyed — the reluctant hero discovers his powers, loses confidence, and then saves the world at the very last second."

"His motivational speech was packed with hackneyed phrases like 'believe in yourself' and 'reach for the stars.'"

"The politician's hackneyed promise to 'fight for ordinary people' convinced nobody in the room."

"Great writing avoids hackneyed metaphors and finds fresh ways to describe familiar feelings."
How hackneyed compares to similar words

Clichéd is the closest word to hackneyed, and the two are nearly interchangeable. The small difference is that a cliché refers specifically to a phrase or expression, while hackneyed is a little broader and can describe ideas, plots, and themes too — not just language.

Trite is also very similar, but trite can additionally suggest that something is overly simplistic or shallow in itself — not just overused.

Banal means dull and unoriginal, but doesn't necessarily imply overuse. Something banal might just be boring because the person had nothing interesting to say, not because their expression got worn out through repetition.

Stale focuses more on freshness — something stale has simply gone past its best. The overuse angle is less central.

A useful rule of thumb: hackneyed = something that was once good, but has been ruined by too much repetition.

Fresh, original, inventive, novel, creative — these are the opposites. A fresh phrase or idea is one that makes you stop, notice, and see something in a new way. It hasn't been worn smooth by a million uses.
Who uses this word, and where?

Hackneyed appears most naturally in writing criticism, book and film reviews, and thoughtful conversation about language or ideas. It has a slightly formal, literary feel to it. In casual everyday speech, most people would simply say "cliché" or "overused." But hackneyed carries a sharper, more precise edge — it specifically points to the damage done by repetition, which is why writers and critics reach for it.
Hackneyed describes a phrase, idea, or expression that was once meaningful but has become dull, empty, and unoriginal because it has been used far too many times.
7383: When you describe someone as haggard, you mean they look extremely exhausted, worn out, and unwell — and it shows clearly on their face.

Haggard is a word used to describe a person's appearance, almost always their face or overall look. A haggard person doesn't just look a little tired — they look like they have been through something hard. Their face looks strained, thin, and drained of life. Think of sunken eyes, hollow or drawn cheeks, a pale complexion, and deep lines of stress or fatigue. It is the look of someone who has been suffering for a while.

This is an important point: haggard is not the word you use when someone looks slightly sleepy after one bad night. It describes a more serious, visible deterioration — the kind that happens after days of no sleep, prolonged worry, serious illness, grief, or relentless overwork. There is a sense that time and hardship have taken a toll on the person, and their face is showing it.

Someone might look haggard because of:

  • Chronic lack of sleep or exhaustion
  • Long-term stress or anxiety
  • A serious or prolonged illness
  • Deep grief or emotional suffering
  • Starvation or physical deprivation

The common thread is that something has been wearing the person down, and their face has started to show the damage.

When you call someone haggard, the tone is usually sympathetic or observational — not cruel. You are noticing that this person looks like they are struggling. A doctor might look at a patient and say they look haggard. A friend who hasn't slept in three days might be described as haggard. The word carries a sense of concern or pity, not mockery.
How it differs from similar words

Several words come close to haggard, but each one has a slightly different focus:

Tired or sleepy just means low on energy. You can feel tired and still look fine. Haggard means the exhaustion is so deep and lasting that it is visible on your face and body.

Gaunt focuses specifically on looking dangerously thin, almost skeletal. A haggard person may or may not be thin — what matters is the overall look of suffering and fatigue.

Weary describes how someone feels — heavy, drained, and lacking motivation. Haggard describes how someone looks.

Drawn is the closest relative to haggard. A drawn face looks tight, strained, and thin from stress. Haggard is slightly stronger and broader — it includes the exhaustion, the pallor, the hollow eyes, the whole picture.

So if tired is a 3 out of 10 on the exhaustion scale, haggard is closer to an 8 or 9 — and crucially, it is always about visible appearance, not just an internal feeling.
How it is used in sentences

Here are natural examples showing how the word works in practice:

  • "After three sleepless nights with a sick child, she looked haggard and pale."
  • "The soldiers returned from the battlefield with haggard faces and distant eyes."
  • "He had lost weight and looked haggard from months of caring for his ailing father."
  • "The detective investigating the case appeared haggard — clearly, he hadn't been home in days."
  • "Her haggard expression told me she had been crying all night."

Notice that the word is almost always paired with something related to the face or appearance: haggard face, haggard look, haggard expression, haggard eyes, looked haggard. That's its natural home.

Haggard is a moderately formal word. You would find it comfortably in a novel, a news article, or careful conversation. It's not slang, and it's not stiff academic language either. It sits right in the middle — educated, clear, and expressive.

Haggard means looking visibly exhausted, worn out, and unwell — especially on the face — as a result of prolonged stress, illness, grief, or lack of sleep.

If you remember that image — a face that looks like it has been through something hard and is showing every bit of it — you will never misuse this word.
7384:
A haggle is a prolonged, back-and-forth negotiation between two people — usually over the price of something — where each side pushes and pulls, trying to get a deal that works in their own favor. Neither side simply accepts the other's first offer. Instead, they go back and forth, proposing, rejecting, counter-offering, until they either agree or give up.

Think of it as a tug-of-war with words and numbers.

The word "haggle" is most commonly known as a verb (meaning: to haggle — the act of doing it). The noun form refers to a specific instance or episode of that activity — one particular negotiation that went through this messy, drawn-out back-and-forth process.

So when you say "a haggle", you're referring to one such episode — a specific, identifiable event of negotiating where both sides bargained persistently.
What a haggle actually looks like

Imagine you walk into a secondhand furniture market. You see a chair priced at ₹5,000. You offer ₹2,500. The seller says no. You say ₹3,000. The seller says ₹4,500. You say ₹3,500. The seller says ₹4,000. You say ₹3,800 final offer. The seller agrees.

That entire exchange — from first offer to final agreement — is a haggle. It had a beginning, a middle (the back-and-forth), and an end.

• It involves two active participants. Both sides are fighting for their interest. If only one person is pushing for a lower price and the other is simply saying "take it or leave it," that's not quite a haggle — a haggle requires genuine back-and-forth from both sides.
  • It takes time and effort. A haggle isn't a quick, one-line negotiation. It implies some persistence, some resistance, some going back and forth. There's a sense of effort involved.
  • It usually ends in compromise. The final agreed price is rarely what either side originally wanted — it lands somewhere in the middle, as a result of the struggle.
  • It is most commonly about price. While you can technically use the word for any back-and-forth dispute, it is most naturally and most often used in the context of buying or selling something — a car, a piece of clothing at a market, a house, a business deal.

"A haggle" carries a slightly informal, everyday tone. It doesn't sound legal or formal like "a negotiation" or "a settlement." It sounds more like something that happens at a street market, between neighbors, or in a casual business setting. It can carry a slight sense of weariness or exasperation — like it was a bit of a struggle — but it is not a negative word. It's simply descriptive.

It is used more commonly in British English than American English, though it's understood everywhere.

• "After a long haggle with the dealer, she finally drove away with the car for a price she was happy with."
  • "The sale almost fell through — there was quite a haggle over who would pay for the repairs."
  • "It was a tough haggle, but both sides eventually shook hands."
  • "He was tired after the haggle and just wanted to go home."
What makes "a haggle" different from similar words

ConceptWhat it implies
A negotiationFormal, structured, professional — could be about anything
A bargain (noun)More often refers to the result (a good deal), not the process itself
A disputeImplies conflict with no necessary intention to reach a deal
A haggleInformal, about price, involves real back-and-forth effort, usually ends in a deal
The key idea to hold onto

A haggle is not just any conversation about price. It is a specific, effortful, back-and-forth episode of bargaining where both sides push hard, neither accepts the first offer, and the process itself takes energy and time before a middle ground is reached. When someone says "it was quite a haggle," they're telling you: that wasn't easy — we really had to fight for it.
7385:
To haggle means to negotiate the price of something by going back and forth with another person — each side pushing for a deal that favors them — until you either agree on a price or give up.

It is not simply asking "can you give me a discount?" once and accepting whatever answer comes. Haggling is a process — a kind of verbal tug-of-war over price, where both sides make offers, counter-offers, and push back, often multiple times, before a final price is settled.

Imagine you are at an open-air market and you see a rug. The seller says it costs $100. You think that is too high, so you say, "I'll give you $60." The seller says, "No, $60 is too low. How about $85?" You say, "I can do $70." The seller says, "$75, and that's my final offer." You agree. Done.

That entire back-and-forth process is haggling.

Notice a few things about what just happened:

Both people participated actively. Haggling is never one-sided. The seller is trying to get as much money as possible. The buyer is trying to pay as little as possible. Both know this, and both play along willingly.

Neither side accepted the first offer. That is the whole point. If you simply paid $100 without question, you did not haggle. If the seller simply said "okay, $60," they did not haggle either. Haggling requires the back-and-forth.

It ends in agreement or walkaway. Sometimes both sides find a price they can live with. Other times, the gap is too wide, one person walks away, and no deal is made.

Haggling is extremely common in open markets, bazaars, flea markets, street stalls, and second-hand shops — anywhere prices are not fixed by a tag or a machine. In many countries and cultures, especially across the Middle East, South Asia, Southeast Asia, Africa, and Latin America, haggling is a completely normal and expected part of everyday buying and selling. Walking up and paying the first price asked would actually seem strange or even foolish.

In Western countries, haggling is less common in everyday shopping (you cannot haggle at a supermarket checkout), but it is very much expected and practiced when buying used cars, houses, antiques, or at garage sales and flea markets. It also happens in business-to-business deals, salary negotiations, and contract discussions.
The Feel and Tone of the Word

"Haggle" carries a slightly informal and sometimes mildly negative tone — it suggests the negotiation is a little stubborn, drawn-out, or petty, not a smooth and professional negotiation. It implies that the people involved are squabbling over small differences, or at least being persistent and scrappy about price.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "The two companies negotiated the contract." — sounds formal and professional.
  • "She haggled with the vendor over the price of a scarf." — sounds informal, a little gritty, very human.

Both describe price negotiation, but "haggle" feels more street-level, more personal, and often more stubborn.

That said, the word is not deeply negative. It is often used with a neutral or even admiring tone — calling someone a good haggler can be a compliment, meaning they are sharp, persistent, and do not get taken advantage of.

It is important not to confuse haggling with:

Just asking for a discount. Asking once — "Could you do $80?" — and accepting whatever they say is not haggling. Haggling means you push back if they say no, and the conversation continues.

Arguing or fighting. Haggling can feel like a mild argument, but it is cooperative at its core. Both sides want to reach a deal. It is not hostile — in cultures where it is common, it can actually be quite friendly and even playful.

Formal negotiation. When executives sit in boardrooms and negotiate, we usually say they are "negotiating," not "haggling." Haggling feels more informal and often involves smaller stakes or more petty back-and-forth.
How It Is Used in Sentences

Here are examples showing the different ways "haggle" appears:

  • She haggled with the street vendor and got the price down from $50 to $30.
  • Don't be embarrassed to haggle — in this market, everyone does it.
  • He spent nearly half an hour haggling over the price of the old bicycle.
  • They haggled back and forth before finally agreeing on a number.
  • I'm not good at haggling; I always end up paying more than I should.

Notice that you commonly see "haggle with" (someone) and "haggle over" (something). These are the two most natural pairings with the word.
To haggle is to negotiate a price through repeated back-and-forth offers and counter-offers, with each side trying to get the better deal, until both agree or one walks away.
7386: A haiku is a very short poem — always three lines — that captures a single, fleeting moment, usually from the natural world. Think of it as a photograph taken with words: not a full story, not an explanation of feelings, but one instant held still so completely that the reader can feel it themselves.

A haiku follows a strict syllable count across its three lines:

  • Line 1: 5 syllables
  • Line 2: 7 syllables
  • Line 3: 5 syllables

That's 17 syllables in total — nothing more, nothing less. Here is an original example:

Rain on the tin roof (5)
A child watches each drop fall (7)
The cat does not move (5)

Count for yourself: Rain-on-the-tin-roof. A-child-watch-es-each-drop-fall. The-cat-does-not-move. This tight constraint is intentional. When you only have 17 syllables, every single word must earn its place.

Three things are almost always present in a traditional haiku:

1. A moment in the present
A haiku lives in right now. It doesn't say "I remembered the rain" or "rain will come tomorrow." It says: this is happening, here, at this moment. The reader is pulled directly into the scene.

2. Something from nature
Traditional haiku is rooted in the natural world — seasons, animals, weather, plants, water, sky. This isn't decoration; nature is the subject itself. The haiku trusts the natural world to carry the meaning.

3. A season word (kigo)
Every traditional haiku contains at least one word that quietly signals which season the poem belongs to. "Cherry blossoms" = spring. "Bare branches" = winter. "Cicadas" = summer. This anchors the poem to a specific, real time of year, which matters deeply in the Japanese tradition the form comes from.
The secret engine of a haiku: the cut

This is what separates a truly great haiku from a merely decent one.

Every haiku has two parts, and between them there is a sudden pause — a break — where the reader's mind makes a small leap. The two parts seem separate at first glance, but placed side by side, they create depth and meaning that neither part could create alone. This technique is called a cut (in Japanese: kireji, which means "cutting word").

Here is an example:

Empty park bench, noon —
Leaves spiral down in silence
Someone was just here

The first line shows an empty bench at midday. The third line introduces the feeling of a recent absence — someone was here moments ago and has now gone. The falling leaves in the middle give everything a mood of quiet passing. None of this is explained in the poem. It just shows you the pieces and lets your mind do the rest. That invisible leap between the two parts — that is the cut.
What haiku deliberately does NOT do

Understanding what haiku avoids is just as important as knowing what it includes.

  • It does not tell you what to feel. It never says "I felt lonely" or "it was beautiful." It shows you something and trusts you to feel it yourself.
  • It does not rhyme. Haiku has no rhyme scheme, unlike much Western poetry.
  • It does not use heavy or decorative language. No elaborate metaphors, no flowery descriptions. The language is plain, direct, and unadorned.
  • It does not explain itself. If a haiku has to explain what it means, it has already failed as a haiku.

Haiku grew out of an older Japanese form called renga — a long, collaborative, linked poem written by multiple poets. The opening verse of a renga (called the hokku) had to be especially strong because it set the tone for everything that followed. Over time, the great Japanese poet Matsuo Basho (1644–1694) took the hokku and made it into a standalone art form. He is considered the father and greatest master of haiku.

After Basho, two other masters refined the form: Yosa Buson (a painter as well as a poet) and Kobayashi Issa (known for compassionate, everyday subjects). Later, in the late 19th century, the poet and critic Masaoka Shiki formally named this standalone verse form "haiku" — giving the word its modern identity. Before Shiki, these poems were still called hokku.

By the 20th century, haiku had spread far beyond Japan and was being written in English, French, Spanish, and dozens of other languages around the world.

As a noun, "haiku" is both singular and plural in its traditional usage, because it comes from Japanese, which doesn't distinguish singular from plural the same way English does:

  • Singular: "She wrote a haiku."
  • Plural: "He read ten haiku." (Casual English also accepts "haikus," and both are widely understood.)

You'll also see it used as a modifier: "a haiku collection," "haiku poetry," "a haiku master," "the haiku tradition."

In the strictest traditional form, haiku must have a season word and be about nature. In modern and English haiku, many poets loosen these rules. Some haiku are about city life, human relationships, or technology. Some poets even argue that the spirit of a haiku — that quality of immediacy, simplicity, and the cut — matters more than the exact 5-7-5 count (since syllables in English work differently from the sound units in Japanese). Both strict and free interpretations are practiced today and considered valid.

There is also a closely related form called senryu, which follows the same 5-7-5 structure but focuses on human nature, behavior, and humor rather than the natural world. Senryu is sometimes confused with haiku, but the two are considered separate forms.

Haiku is a training in attention. It says: this small thing — a falling leaf, a rain drop, an empty bench — deserves your complete, undivided focus. The whole art of haiku is slowing down enough to notice one moment fully, then finding the fewest possible words to pass that noticing on to another person. In that sense, a haiku is not just a poem. It is a practice of paying attention to the world.
7387:
Hail is precipitation — something that falls from the sky — but unlike rain (which is liquid water) or snow (which is soft, fluffy ice crystals), hail is made of solid lumps of ice. These lumps are called hailstones.

Hailstones are hard, compact, and dense — more like little ice rocks than anything soft. They can be as small as a pea or as large as a golf ball. In extreme storms, hailstones the size of a cricket ball or even larger have been recorded, though that is rare.

How it works:
Inside a powerful thunderstorm, there are violent upward winds called updrafts. These winds blast water droplets high up into the freezing upper atmosphere. The droplets freeze into a tiny ball of ice. The updrafts then keep tossing this ball up and down inside the cloud. Each time it rises back into the freezing zone, a new layer of ice coats it — like dipping a ball repeatedly in water and letting it freeze. Eventually, the hailstone gets too heavy for the updraft to hold up, and it plummets to the ground.

This is why, if you cut a hailstone open, you can see concentric rings (rings one inside another, like an onion) — each ring represents one cycle of freezing.

Important grammar note:
"Hail" in this sense is an uncountable noun (also called a mass noun). You cannot say "three hails fell." Instead, you say:

  • "Hail fell during the storm."
  • "The hail damaged the roof."

When you want to refer to individual pieces, you use the word hailstone (countable): "Several large hailstones shattered the windshield."

Related compound words you'll encounter:

  • Hailstone — a single piece of hail.
  • Hailstorm — a storm during which hail falls.
  • Hailstrike / hail damage — damage caused by falling hailstones.

Why it matters in real life:
Hail is genuinely destructive. A heavy hailstorm can:

  • Flatten crops and ruin harvests entirely
  • Dent and crack car roofs and hoods
  • Smash greenhouse glass and solar panels
  • Injure people or animals caught outdoors
The Figurative (Extended) Meaning — A Torrent of Things

Because hailstones fall in great numbers, rapidly, all at once, and forcefully, the word "hail" is also used figuratively to describe a large, sudden, overwhelming quantity of things coming at you all at once — especially things that feel like an attack.

This use always follows the structure: "a hail of [something]"

Examples:

  • "The soldiers walked into a hail of bullets."
    → So many bullets flying at once, it was like a storm of them.
  • "The politician faced a hail of criticism after the speech."
    → A sudden, overwhelming burst of criticism from many directions.
  • "The goalkeeper was pelted with a hail of snowballs."
    → Many snowballs thrown all at once, rapidly.

The things described this way are usually numerous, fast, and overwhelming — not a single item, but a barrage. You wouldn't say "a hail of one complaint." The imagery is always of many things hitting at once, the way hailstones do.
A Rare, Mostly Archaic Meaning — A Call or Shout

In older English, "hail" was also used as a noun meaning a shout to get someone's attention, especially from a distance — like calling out to a passing ship. You may still encounter the phrase "within hail", meaning within shouting distance (close enough that your shout would be heard). This use is largely obsolete in everyday modern speech, but you might find it in older literature or nautical writing.

7388: The verb "hail" has three distinct meanings in English, each used in a completely different situation. Once you understand all three, you'll never be confused by this word again.
Meaning 1: To call out to someone, or to signal for attention

This is the most everyday meaning. When you "hail" someone, you call out to them loudly, or make a visible signal to get their attention — usually because they are at a distance from you, or moving away.

Examples:

  • She hailed a taxi. (She raised her hand and called out to stop a passing cab.)
  • He hailed me from across the street. (He called out loudly to get my attention from far away.)
  • The sailor hailed the passing ship. (He called out to the ship's crew to get their notice.)

The key feeling here: There is always a sense of reaching across a gap — a distance, a crowd, or movement. You aren't whispering to someone right beside you. You're making an effort to be noticed or heard.

Common collocations (word pairings) to remember:

  • Hail a cab / taxi — this is a very fixed, classic phrase
  • Hail a passing ship / vehicle
  • Hail someone from a distance
Meaning 2: To publicly praise or declare someone/something as great

This is perhaps the richest and most powerful meaning of the verb. When someone or something is "hailed," they are publicly celebrated, recognized, or declared to be something impressive — a hero, a genius, a success, a breakthrough, and so on.

Think of it as an announcement with excitement and admiration behind it. It's not a quiet compliment from one person in private. It's a bold, public declaration.

The most important pattern to know:

hail + someone/something + as + [noun or description]

Examples:

  • The scientists were hailed as heroes. (The public celebrated them as heroes loudly and widely.)
  • The new drug was hailed as a miracle. (Everyone called it a miracle, with great enthusiasm.)
  • Critics hailed the novel as the greatest book of the decade. (Critics publicly declared it to be extraordinary.)
  • She was hailed as a genius by her professors. (Her professors publicly and enthusiastically recognized her as a genius.)

The key feeling here: "Hailing" someone as something carries weight. It implies widespread recognition, not just one person's opinion. When the media, the public, experts, or a group "hail" someone, they are collectively lifting that person or thing up.

Notice: This meaning is very often used in the passive voice — "was hailed as," "were hailed as" — because the focus is on the person or thing being celebrated, not on who is doing the celebrating.
Meaning 3: To originally come from a place (always in the phrase "hail from")

This meaning is always and only used in the fixed phrase "hail from." It simply means to come from a particular place — your hometown, your country of origin, the city where a band was formed, and so on.

Examples:

  • She hails from a small town in Italy. (She originally comes from that town.)
  • The band hails from Detroit. (The band originally comes from Detroit.)
  • He hails from a long line of farmers. (He comes from a family background of farmers.)

The key feeling here: "Hail from" is slightly more formal or expressive than simply saying "come from." It adds a touch of pride or character — as if where someone comes from is part of their identity.

Important: This meaning is locked into the phrase "hail from." You cannot swap "from" for another preposition here. You would never say "hail of" or "hail at" to express this idea.
Bonus Meaning: When hail (ice) falls from the sky

Because "hail" is also a noun for the ice pellets that fall during storms, the verb form is used in one simple weather expression:

  • It is hailing outside. (Hailstones are falling from the sky right now.)

This works exactly like "it is raining" or "it is snowing." It's impersonal and straightforward, and you'll only ever use it this way.

Here's a quick mental map to keep the three main meanings straight:

  • Hail a taxi → You are calling out / signaling for something.
  • Hailed as a hero → Someone is being publicly praised and celebrated.
  • Hails from Texas → Someone originally comes from a place.

And the extra one:

  • It's hailing → Ice is falling from the sky.

1. "Hailed as" vs. simply "praised"
When someone is "hailed as" something, it implies more than ordinary praise. It suggests that many people agree, that the recognition is widespread, and that the person or thing truly stands out. You wouldn't "hail" your friend for passing an ordinary exam. You'd hail a scientist whose discovery changed the world.

2. The passive voice dominates Meaning 2
You will see "was hailed as" and "were hailed as" far more often than the active voice. This is natural — the emphasis is almost always on the person being celebrated, not on the people doing the celebrating.

3. "Hail from" sounds slightly formal or literary
In casual conversation, people usually just say "come from." But "hail from" appears often in journalism, introductions, and writing. Saying "She hails from a small fishing village in Norway" sounds richer and more characterful than "She comes from a small fishing village in Norway."

4. Hailing a person vs. hailing a vehicle
When you hail a vehicle (a taxi, a bus, a ship), you're physically signaling it to stop. When you hail a person, you're calling out to get their attention. The action is similar — you're making yourself noticed — but the goal is slightly different.

That covers everything about the verb "hail" — all its meanings, patterns, nuances, and common uses. You now have the complete picture.
7389:
"Hail from" simply means "to come from" or "to originate from" a particular place. When you say someone hails from somewhere, you are telling people where that person was born, grew up, or considers their original home.

Think of it this way: if someone asks, "Where do you hail from?" — they are asking, "Where are you originally from?"

Examples:

  • "She hails from a small town in Italy." → She originally comes from a small town in Italy.
  • "He hails from New York City." → His hometown, or place of origin, is New York City.
  • "The band hails from Liverpool." → The band originally comes from Liverpool.
Where Did This Phrase Come From? (Its Origin)

To truly understand a phrase, it helps to know where it was born. The story of "hail from" is fascinating.

The Word "Hail"

The word "hail" is very old. It comes from the Old Norse word "heill," which meant health, good luck, or well-being. This is why, even today, we say "Hail!" as a shout of greeting or honor — like "Hail the king!" It is a way of acknowledging someone loudly and proudly.

So "hail" means to call out to someone, to greet them, or to acknowledge them.

The Nautical (Sailing) Connection

The phrase "hail from" was born at sea. In the age of sailing ships, when two ships came near each other on the ocean, the sailors needed to know who the other ship was and where it had come from. One crew would shout across the water — they would hail the other ship.

The full question they called out was something like:

"Ship ahoy! Where do you hail from?"

This meant: "What is your home port? Where did your journey begin?"

Over time, this nautical phrase jumped from the ocean to everyday life. People started using "hail from" to ask not just where a ship came from, but where a person came from. The expression stuck, and that is why we still use it today.
What Exactly Does "Hail From" Refer To?

This is an important question. "Hail from" can refer to:

1. Where you were born

"She hails from Mumbai" — she was born in Mumbai.

2. Where you grew up

Even if you were born somewhere else, you might hail from the place where you spent your childhood and think of as home.

3. Your hometown or place of origin

This is the most common use. It simply means the place you call home, the place you identify with as your roots.

The phrase focuses on origin and roots — not where you currently live. For example, someone might currently live in London but hail from a small village in Scotland. Those are two different things.
Can "Hail From" Be Used for Things, Not Just People?

Yes, absolutely! "Hail from" can describe the origin of things, ideas, traditions, or organizations — not just people.

  • "This spice hails from ancient India." → This spice originally comes from ancient India.
  • "The tradition hails from medieval Europe." → The tradition originated in medieval Europe.
  • "The recipe hails from a remote village in Mexico." → The recipe has its roots in that village.

This is perfectly natural and correct English.

"Hail from" sits in a comfortable middle ground — it is not too formal and not slang. It is used in:

  • Everyday conversation ("Oh, where do you hail from?")
  • News articles ("The scientist, who hails from South Korea, won the prize.")
  • Biographies and introductions ("The author hails from rural Canada.")
  • Speeches and presentations

It carries a slightly distinguished or respectful tone compared to simply saying "come from." When someone says you hail from a place, there is a tiny sense of pride or acknowledgment baked into it — almost as if your origin is something worth noting. This connects back to its roots in the old "Hail!" greeting, which was always a proud, loud acknowledgment.
"Hail From" vs. "Come From" — What Is the Difference?

These two phrases mean nearly the same thing, and you can often use them interchangeably. However, there is a subtle difference in feel:

"Come from" is plain, neutral, and purely informational.
→ "I come from Brazil."

"Hail from" carries a slightly richer, more distinguished, or emphatic tone. It can also sound a little more literary or proud.
→ "I hail from Brazil."

Neither is wrong. But if you want to sound slightly more expressive or polished, "hail from" is the more characterful choice.
Grammar: How to Use It Correctly

The structure is simple:

[Subject] + hail(s) from + [Place]

Pay attention to the -s for he/she/it:

  • I hail from Argentina.
  • You hail from Argentina.
  • He / She / It hails from Argentina. (Don't forget the -s!)
  • We hail from Argentina.
  • They hail from Argentina.

In the Past Tense:

Use "hailed from" when talking about someone who has died or something historical.

  • "The great composer hailed from Vienna." (He is no longer alive, so past tense.)
  • "The ancient tradition hailed from a time when..."

As a Question:

  • "Where do you hail from?" → Where are you originally from?
  • "Where does she hail from?" → Where is she originally from?

One Final Way to Remember It

Picture an old sailor on a ship, cupping his hands around his mouth and shouting proudly across the water: "We hail from Portsmouth!" — announcing loudly and proudly where his ship's home is.

That proud, loud announcement of origin — that is the soul of "hail from." Every time you use it or hear it, you are carrying a tiny piece of seafaring history with you.
